questions.question: What is the Jacobian determinant of $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2-y^2,\ 2xy)$ at $(1,-1)$?
How is the total derivative related to the Jacobian matrix when $f$ is differentiable?
options: The existence of the Jacobian always implies total differentiability.
If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable, its total derivative is equal to the Jacobian matrix.
The total derivative is always represented by the transpose of the Jacobian matrix.
The total derivative equals the Jacobian only when $\boldsymbol{f}$ is linear.

questions.question: Why must $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ be an interior point of $\boldsymbol{E}$ for the Jacobian?
options: It guarantees that every partial derivative of $\boldsymbol{f}$ exists at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
It ensures $\boldsymbol{f}$ is defined near $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ in every coordinate direction.
It guarantees that $\boldsymbol{f}$ is totally differentiable at the point $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
It makes the Jacobian at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ a square matrix, so it can be inverted.

questions.question: For $\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k$, what is the size of the Jacobian matrix?
What entries appear in the Jacobian matrix?
options: Partial derivatives of the component functions with respect to input variables.
Only the values of the component functions at the chosen input point.
Second-order partial derivatives of the component functions in pairs of inputs.
Partial derivatives of the input variables with respect to the component functions.

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y$, what is the Jacobian row at $(1,2)$?
For $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x+y,xy)$, which entry is in row $2$, column $1$ of the Jacobian?
For $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y^2,x+y)$, what is the size of the Jacobian?

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ be an interior point of $E$ and let $\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k$ have all first-order partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$. Which conclusion is justified by this alone?
options: The Jacobian matrix $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ can be written down.
$\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ is the matrix of the linear map that best approximates $\boldsymbol{f}$ near $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}$ be scalar-valued on $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with all partial derivatives at the interior point $\boldsymbol{x}_0$. What is its Jacobian matrix $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$?
options: The $n\times n$ matrix of second-order partial derivatives of $f$.
The $1\times1$ matrix containing the sum $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{f}\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^k$ with $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ have all partial derivatives at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$. What does row $i$ of $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{J}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$ contain?
options: The transposed gradient $\nabla f_i(\boldsymbol{x}_0)^{\top}$ of the single component $f_i$.
The partial derivatives of all components with respect to the single input $x_i$.
The second-order partial derivatives of the component $f_i$.
